title: Why Orcas Give Up Their Kill When Pilot Whales Show Up
alt_titles: Why Orcas Leave Their Kill to Get Away From Pilot Whales
How Doug Would Die Dressed as an Orca Among Pilot Whales
Off Iceland, Pilot Whales Chase the Scariest Hunter at Sea
Scientists Saw Orcas Drop Their Kill and Flee Pilot Whales
thumbnail_brief: A tight wall of black, round-headed pilot whales charging left to right, a large orca fleeing out of frame ahead of them with a sweat drop, and tiny Doug in the orca costume (cap on top) caught between the two looking back at the pod, so the title's 'give up their kill' gets its twist from WRONG WAY (never ORCA, PILOT, WHALE, KILL, RUN or any title word; no contact, no bite, no injured whale; no size-ratio label; no calf).
description:
Off Iceland, when long-finned pilot whales move in on orcas, the orcas usually leave, sometimes at full speed and sometimes abandoning a meal, even though they are much bigger. Doug, dressed as an orca, finds out why the ocean's top predator backs off from pilot whales, from a speaker playing killer whale sounds to a deep-sea sprint, a raided longline, a following shark, a sperm whale standoff and the pilot whale family itself.

Where should we send Doug next? Tell us in the comments.
Subscribe. Doug's death counter only ever goes one way.
